extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of sociology/economic theory; general readers interested in social class and status
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and assess social-economic indicators of leisure and reputability (signs of status) such as trophies, immaterial accomplishments, manners, servants, and conspicuous consumption as described in a sociological/theoretical account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangible products as lasting evidence of productive labour
rubrics_metrics.description: The lasting evidence of productive labour is its material product--commonly some article of consumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economic point of view: productive labour leaves a material product that can be exhibited as proof of labour; trophies or booty serve analogous roles for exploit. Tangible products function as demonstrable proof of prior productive effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Badges/insignia/trophies as symbols of exploit or honour
rubrics_metrics.description: It is customary to assume some badge of insignia of honour that will serve as a conventionally accepted mark of exploit, and which at the same time indicates the quantity or degree of exploit of which it is the symbol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: heraldic devices, medals, honorary decorations. These serve as conventional marks to measure and compare degrees of exploit or status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immaterial goods as criteria of past leisure
rubrics_metrics.description: Leisure...does not commonly leave a material product. The criteria of a past performance of leisure therefore commonly take the form of 'immaterial' goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include knowledge of dead languages, occult sciences, correct spelling, syntax and prosody, domestic music, knowledge of dress/furniture, games, sports, and breeding of animals. Such accomplishments survive only when they serve as evidence of non-productive time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manners, breeding, polite usage and decorum as evidence of leisure
rubrics_metrics.description: Manners and breeding, polite usage, decorum, and formal and ceremonial observances...are more widely and more imperatively insisted on as required evidences of a reputable degree of leisure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These social facts are immediately presented and hence strongly enforced as marks of the leisure class; their presence signals time and resources devoted to non-productive refinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conformity to ceremonial code (punctilios) as a mark of status
rubrics_metrics.description: All that class of ceremonial observances which are classed under the general head of manners hold a more important place in the esteem of men during the stage of culture at which conspicuous leisure has the greatest vogue as a mark of reputability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ceremonial code's observance is especially valued in status-oriented cultures; its decay signals vulgarisation. Continental examples illustrate communities where punctilios retain archaic force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decorum's apparent intrinsic utility vs its economic ground
rubrics_metrics.description: Decorum...came to be possessed of a substantial utility in themselves; but their ulterior, economic ground is to be sought in the honorific character of that leisure or non-productive employment of time and effort without which good manners are not acquired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although decorum is felt as intrinsically right (breach is odious), its deeper function is as a voucher for leisure: acquiring decorum requires time, application, and expense, thereby signaling pecuniary standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time, application and expense required to acquire good breeding
rubrics_metrics.description: Good breeding requires time, application and expense, and can therefore not be compassed by those whose time and energy are taken up with work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possession of refined tastes and manners is prima facie evidence of leisure because they imply a substantial, patent waste of time in their acquisition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visible/tangible results or marks to evidence leisure not performed publicly
rubrics_metrics.description: So much of the honourable life of leisure as is not spent in the sight of spectators can serve the purposes of reputability only in so far as it leaves a tangible, visible result that can be put in evidence and can be measured and compared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: habitual bearing, carriage, accomplishments or consciously cultivated marks of leisure. Passive habituation or active assiduous acquisition both create observable signs for comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assiduous acquisition and mimicry (snobbery) as route to cultured status
rubrics_metrics.description: The possibility of producing pathological and other idiosyncrasies of person and manner by shrewd mimicry and a systematic drill have been turned to account in the deliberate production of a cultured class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Syncopated evolution of gentle birth via imitation and training (snobbery) can yield serviceable results equal to prolonged hereditary leisure; deliberate cultivation of marks of gentility is a recognized pathway.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurable degrees of conformity to canons of taste
rubrics_metrics.description: There are, moreover, measureable degrees of conformity to the latest accredited code of the punctilios as regards decorous means and methods of consumption...persons may be graded and scheduled with some accuracy and effect according to a progressive scale of manners and breeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standards of taste are supervised by the law of conspicuous leisure and evolve to better reflect its requirements; proximate grounds may vary but the abiding test remains wasteful expenditure of time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between courtesy (goodwill) and properties (status expressions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Much of the courtesy of everyday intercourse is of course a direct expression of consideration and kindly good-will...but the same is not true of the code of properties. These latter are expressions of status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bearing toward menials and superiors encodes relations of dominance/subservience; comportment of the well-bred signals status beyond mere goodwill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership of persons (servants/slaves) as evidence of wealth and dominance
rubrics_metrics.description: The institution of ownership has begun with the ownership of persons...The incentives to acquiring such property have apparently been: (1) a propensity for dominance and coercion; (2) the utility of these persons as evidence of the prowess of the owner; (3) the utility of their services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In earlier cultural stages women and other slaves function as units of value and investment; possession itself is a public sign of wealth and power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of labour that exempts certain persons from productive labour
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal service and attendance on the master becomes the special office of a portion of the servants, while those who are wholly employed in industrial occupations proper are removed more and more from all immediate relation to the person of their owner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wives (chief wife) and personal attendants become exempt from productive industry as status rises; exemption breadth depends on closeness to master's person and wealth available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialised body servants as conspicuous evidence rather than utilitarian labour
rubrics_metrics.description: These specialised servants are useful more for show than for service actually performed...their office includes continually fewer duties, and their service tends in the end to become nominal only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preference for male, lusty, personable attendants because they are more powerful and more expensive; specialization and multiplication of servants increase display of master's ability to waste time and resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vicarious leisure (servants' leisure performed for master's reputability)
rubrics_metrics.description: The leisure of the servant class exempt from productive labour is in some sort a performance exacted from them, and is not normally or primarily directed to their own comfort. The leisure of the servant is not his own leisure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vicarious leisure is performed for the reputability of the master/household; it includes trained display, formal observances, and consumption that signal the master's standing rather than the servant's wellbeing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Servant training in subservience and good form as signal of master's means
rubrics_metrics.description: The first requisite of a good servant is that he should conspicuously know his place...he must above all, know how to effect these results in due form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An under-trained servant suggests the master's inability to pay; trained facility in the 'tactics of subservience' is prized because it indicates prolonged vicarious leisure and expense in training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestic duties and household apparatus as forms of vicarious leisure
rubrics_metrics.description: The proximate reason for keeping domestic servants...is (ostensibly) that the members of the household are unable without discomfort to compass the work required by such a modern establishment...Under the requirement of conspicuous consumption of goods, the apparatus of living has grown so elaborate and cumbrous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social duties (calls, drives, clubs, charity) plus elaborate household apparatus make household labour onerous and justify hired service; much domestic labour is ceremonial and counted as vicarious leisure when performed by others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conspicuous consumption of goods as an evidence of pecuniary strength
rubrics_metrics.description: Specialised consumption of goods as an evidence of pecuniary strength had begun to work out in a more or less elaborate system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forms include wearing of liveries, spacious servants' quarters, consumption of food/clothing/dwelling/furniture by lady and household; such consumption is a systematized signal of wealth and status.
